text: The research of Noah's Ark has been 100% confirmed. Noah's Ark has just been 100% confirmed. Allegedly, scientists have found Noah's Ark and are drilling into it now. A team of researchers claim they're just months away from proving they've found Noah's Ark. World-ending biblical structures are coming out of hiding. If you have been online recently, you may have seen videos suggesting that Noah's Ark has been discovered in Turkey. Huge channels with millions of subscribers covered the breaking news. Even the Daily Mail, a news outlet with more than 25 million followers, posted that Noah's Ark resting place 100% confirmed after 4,300 years. But unfortunately, or fortunately, it isn't confirmed. Some of the supposed proof from this very site was examined and rejected decades ago. And here's a rather suspicious coincidence. One of the groups conducting the new research and promoting the story to the press is selling relatively pricey guided Noah's Ark tours. But let's take it one step at a time. First, nobody has dug up a ship. In 1959, Turkish army captain Ilhan Durupinar noticed a boat-shaped formation in aerial photographs of eastern Turkey near Mount Ararat. It was named after him. It's about 515 feet long, close to the Ark's biblical length of 300 cubits if you use a longer ancient cubit. So I can see why that caught people's attention. In 1960, it even made it into the Life magazine, and the team led by Dorj Vandeman, a Seventh-day Adventist evangelist, went to investigate. They dug into the site but found no visible archaeological remains. Their public conclusion was that it appeared to be a natural formation. These were people looking for the Ark, and even they couldn't confirm it. But believers kept coming back. In the late 1970s, Ron Wyatt, a Seventh-day Adventist who believed the Bible story were literal history, started promoting the site as Noah's Ark. He claimed to have found petrified wood, metal feedings, and nearby stones that served as anchors. In the 1980s, another Ark researcher, David Fassel, investigated alongside Wyatt and initially supported the claim. That matters because he later took another look at the evidence. Meanwhile, investigators used radar and, in 1988, drilled four holes into the formation. So the idea that nobody has drilled there before is simply wrong. Those investigations didn't establish that there was a wooden ship underground. Then, in 1996, Fassel co-authored a geological paper with Lawrence Collins. They examined alleged ship materials. Supposed wood turned out to be rock, and alleged iron feeding was naturally occurring minerals. The supposed anchor stones matched rock from the region. Their conclusion? The boat shape was produced by geology, not shipbuilding. And yet, every few years, Noah's Ark is discovered again. For example, three years ago, Dylan Page, the Daily Mail's arch-nemesis, covered claims about this formation. So, what changed now? The new work involves deeper drilling and more samples. Fair enough, it could tell us something. But researchers already drilled there in 1988, brought up samples of the rock and soil beneath the formation, and concluded it was natural. So, could there be another explanation for the headlines? Well, there's one extremely suspicious detail. Noah's Ark scans help fund the university-led research and promotes it with the press. Coincidentally, they also sell guided tours to that place for thousands of dollars. I'm not the Daily Mail, so I'm not going to claim anything with 100% certainty, But when potential customers include Christians hoping for physical proof of a story sacred to them, suggesting that proof might be buried at your tour's destination is pretty convenient. Maybe they sincerely believe that over a span of more than 65 years, all the researchers who concluded this was a natural formation somehow got it wrong. Maybe it is simply good marketing. Either way, until the new samples provide even a shred of evidence of a man-made structure at the site, let alone Noah's Ark, 100% confirmed should make you more suspicious than convinced.
